While the Trump plan promises to encourage people to stay in Gaza, Israeli right-wing politicians have stepped up calls for the mass removal of Palestinians through “voluntary emigration”. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said last month there was "[USN:L6N44W0HN TEXT:"no real solution"] for Gaza in the end without this migration". Israel's defence ministry in 2025 established an office tasked with overseeing “voluntary emigration” from Gaza, after comments by Trump suggesting Gazans [USN:S0N3OH00C TEXT:"could be permanently displaced"]. Trump later backed away from the idea, which faced strong resistance from Arab states and was widely rejected internationally. Israeli officials have said there are no plans to move Gaza's population out by force. Israel will hold a general election on October 27, the country's first since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. Some leading opposition figures have spoken in support of Trump's plan. Polls show pro- and anti-Netanyahu parties in a tight race.

item.title: Brazil ex-President Bolsonaro wins big without his name on the ballot
item.description: Flavio Bolsonaro's shock victory represented a stunning reversal of his father's fortunes as the rehabilitated Bolsonaro family and ideological movement emerged stronger than ever.
item.dc:creator: Luciana Magalhaes, Ricardo Brito
item.content:encoded: The biggest winner in Brazil's blockbuster weekend election did not even appear on the ballot. [USN:L1N38M126 TEXT:"Banned from public office"], former President Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest, serving a [USN:S0N3UJ08N TEXT:"27-year sentence"] for a coup plot after his 2022 election loss. The 71-year-old watched from confinement on Sunday as his eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, scored an upset victory over leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the first round of the presidential election. The result, which pundits linked to a right-wing wave sweeping the region and Lula's own campaign missteps, made Flavio the favorite to win second-round voting on October 25. The shock victory represented a stunning reversal of his father's fortunes as the rehabilitated Bolsonaro family and ideological movement emerged stronger than ever. Candidates from Bolsonaro's right-wing Liberal Party won up and down the ballot, demonstrating growing traction for the brand despite his legal woes, which the new [USN:L1N45L166 TEXT:"right-wing Congress"] could resolve when it takes office in January. Along with Flavio's surprising success, four more members of the family won public office on Sunday including Senate seats for Michelle Bolsonaro, the ex-president's wife, and second son Carlos while brother Renato and youngest son Jair Renan took seats in the lower house. "In Brazilian political history, I do not remember any political clan that ever managed to elect so many members all at once," said political analyst Antonio Flavio Testa, who served on the former president's transition team in 2018. When the imprisoned ex-president [USN:L1N3XB0QD TEXT:"tapped his son"] to run for Brazil's highest office in December, markets tumbled and center-right allies turned up their noses. Flavio enlisted a little-known lawmaker from his own party, Alfredo Gaspar, as running mate because no other major party would join the ticket. Flavio's most important ally could not appear in public even virtually to campaign for him but still loomed large over the race. An AI-generated avatar of the elder Bolsonaro gave a [USN:L1N43T0Q4 TEXT:"controversial endorsement"] of Flavio at his campaign launch. The real Jair Bolsonaro has moved from serving his sentence in prison to house arrest since March due to ill health including complications from a 2018 stabbing. The Supreme Court prohibited visits from his eldest son for the past three months. Their Liberal Party nearly doubled its bloc in the 81-seat Senate on Sunday to 28 seats, [USN:L6N45R137 TEXT:"the strongest result for a party"] since Brazil's constitution was enacted in the 1980s after the country's return to democracy. That will put amnesty for the elder Bolsonaro at the top of Congress' agenda next year, according to a close aide of Flavio who requested anonymity to speak openly. A vote on the matter could come even sooner if Flavio wins and the current Congress decides to curry favor with the incoming government. Flavio said in early September that he hoped he would be inaugurated with his father present. "I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro," he said. Bolsonaro and Lula, who got 47% and 45% of Sunday's vote respectively, go head-to-head in a second-round vote that political consulting firm Think Policy said would be "very difficult, but not impossible" for Lula to win. To do that, Lula needs to get 62% of voters who backed conservative candidates other than Flavio in the first round, Think Policy estimated. With prospects for Flavio's victory promising, Liberal Party President Valdemar da Costa Neto told Reuters that the elder Bolsonaro could once again play a role in government under his son.

item.title: Argentina, Uruguay, Chile and Brazil submit joint bid to host 2035 World Cup
item.description: Argentina, Uruguay, Chile and Brazil have submitted a joint bid to host the Rugby World Cup in 2035, hoping to bring the quadrennial tournament to South America for the first time, the Argentine Rugby Union (UAR) said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Argentina, Uruguay, Chile and Brazil have submitted a joint bid to host the Rugby World Cup in 2035, hoping to bring the quadrennial tournament to South America for the first time, the Argentine Rugby Union (UAR) said on Monday. The bid outlines plans to stage games in 11 stadiums across 10 cities, with eight venues in Argentina and one each in the other three countries, including the iconic Maracana in Rio de Janeiro. Spain and Japan have also expressed interest in hosting the tournament. World Rugby will undertake site visits and feasibility assessments before identifying a preferred host by next May, with a final decision expected in November 2027. "We have the opportunity to show the world our passion for this sport, our ability to host major events, and everything our countries have to offer," UAR President Felix Paez Molina said in a statement. "We take on this challenge firmly believing that our region deserves an opportunity of this size. "It's a project we're excited about, and we're building it together with the region's Unions and Sudamerica Rugby. Our hope is that, for the first time, a Rugby World Cup can be played in this part of the world." The next World Cup will be held in Australia in 2027, with the tournament making its first foray into the Americas in 2031 when it will be hosted by the United States. Argentina are the most successful rugby-playing nation in the Americas with the Pumas having reached the semi-finals of the World Cup three times in 2007, 2015 and 2023. Uruguay have competed at five editions, while Chile made their debut in 2023 and Brazil have yet to qualify for the tournament.

item.title: Drone sinks ship in Bulgaria's Black Sea - media reports
item.description: Drones sunk one ship and damaged another in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, local media reports said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Drones sunk one ship and damaged another in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, local media reports said. The reports said that the vessels were merchant ships. It was not clear if anyone was injured or killed and a rescue operation was underway, they said. The office of President Iliana Iotova confirmed the attack in the NATO member in an emailed statement, but did not provide details. It is not yet clear who was responsible and the government declined to comment. Prime Minister Rumen Radev is convening a meeting today with key ministries and the security services over the attack and is expected to issue a statement. The drone attack comes after [USN:L1N45R0CZ TEXT:"two people died"] on a ship in the Black Sea outside Romania's territorial waters. Since the Ukraine-Russia war started four years ago, European countries have seen Russian drones breaching their airspace as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and energy routes.

item.title: Pacific leaders watch Tuvalu reclamation effort ahead of UN climate meet
item.description: Representatives of 30 nations watched on Tuesday as white sand dredged from an atoll lagoon was used to reclaim land from the ocean in a fight by the tiny Pacific nation of Tuvalu to keep its main island from being lost to rising waves.
item.dc:creator: Peter Hobson
item.content:encoded: Representatives of 30 nations watched on Tuesday as white sand dredged from an atoll lagoon was used to reclaim land from the ocean in a fight by the tiny Pacific nation of Tuvalu to keep its main island from being lost to rising waves. A group of coral island clusters with about 10,000 inhabitants whose land is on average just 2 m (7 ft) above sea level, Tuvalu is one of the nations most vulnerable to climate change. "You are standing on frontline soil," Foreign Minister Paulson Panapa told the leaders gathered ahead of pre-COP, a preparatory conference for the United Nations COP31 climate forum in Turkey in November. "Promises will not hold back rising tides ... what this moment requires is decisive delivery." Tuesday's reclamation effort, spread over six hectares (14 acres), is part of work costing about $50 million of donor funds that also built sea walls and barriers to protect land. "We are sinking," said Faiva Namoliki, a 39-year-old architect huddled in a sodden jacket in pouring rain outside the event. "Here they see the reality," he said of the visitors. "We hope they will carry those messages away with them and it will make a difference." RISING SEA LEVELS Sea levels around Tuvalu have risen about 15 cm (6 inches) in the three decades to 2023, say NASA researchers, or twice as rapid as the global average. "Small amounts of sea level rise make a very big difference in making flood events bigger and more damaging," Jamie Ovia, the head of Tuvalu’s climate change department, told the leaders. "If we add just 30 cm (12 inches) of sea level rise - expected by 2050 - this supercharges the flooding and makes it drastically bigger than floods we would have seen every 100 years in the past." Such inundations would be economically crippling, he added. Pre-COP events are typically technocratic meetings of climate negotiators but Australia, which is leading the talks this year, aimed with its Pacific partners to highlight the issue of rising sea levels through the Tuvalu gathering. It also seeks to bolster Australia's ties in the region and counter growing Chinese influence. But attendance fell [USN:L8N45M07Y TEXT:"short"], with 11 of the Australian government's tally of 14 attending presidents and prime hailing from Pacific islands. The rest came from Australia, Mauritius and East Timor. Dignitaries arrived amid heavy rains, to be handed umbrellas as they descended from aircraft in matching bright blue patterned shirts, before a traditional song performance by dancers, drummers and singers with flower headbands. SIGNIFICANT ADDITIONS TO LAND MASS The project highlighted on Tuesday is the third in a series that will soon have added about 21 hectares (52 acres) to Tuvalu's main island, project manager Alan Resture told the visitors. The additions are significant in a nation with a total landmass of around 26 sq km (10 sq miles), about twice the size of a large airport. Pacific nations have been at the forefront of efforts to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees to avoid its worst effects - a threshold the world is set to exceed in the coming years. "Every fraction of a degree matters," Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the visiting leaders. Australia is bankrolling pre-COP but has also drawn fire as a major exporter of coal and gas that continues to approve approve fossil projects. "Here in Tuvalu we are seeing what action can look like," said Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. "It's about people."

item.title: Events firm Informa to buy Clarion for £2.24 billion from Blackstone
item.description: Britain's Informa said on Tuesday it would buy events organiser Clarion for £2.24 billion ($3 billion) and separate its Taylor & Francis academic publishing arm, as CEO Stephen Carter focuses on expanding the group's fast-growing live events business.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Britain's Informa (INF.L) said on Tuesday it would buy events organiser Clarion for £2.24 billion ($3 billion) and separate its Taylor & Francis academic publishing arm, as CEO Stephen Carter focuses on expanding the group's fast-growing live events business. The world's largest exhibitions group proposed raising £940 million in new equity to partly fund the acquisition of UK-based Clarion, which owns more than 100 business-to-business live event brands, including consumer electronics event IFA Berlin. US private equity firm Blackstone (BX.N) [USN:L5N3QP0TO TEXT:" last year launched"] a process to sell Clarion, sources told Reuters. The deal would be one of Informa's largest acquisitions in recent years. In 2018, Informa acquired conference organiser UBM for £3.8 billion. It also marks the latest deal-making in the exhibitions industry, which has seen live events roaring back after the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the sector. New York-based Searchlight Capital said in May it would invest in [USN:L6N41E0J1 TEXT:"CloserStill"] Media, in a deal giving it joint control alongside existing investor Providence. The combined B2B live events business is expected to hold more than 1,000 brands across more than 40 market categories in over 30 countries, Informa said. ACADEMIC ARM SEPARATION Informa said it had launched a formal separation process to review all options for Taylor & Francis — whose annual revenue is approaching $1 billion and growing at about 4% — and would report the outcome alongside its full-year results in March 2027. Taylor & Francis has been a beneficiary of AI companies using research to train their models. In 2024, its performance was boosted by data access agreements with AI companies, although a lower rate of revenue contribution last year had hurt its underlying performance. The business, which accounted for about 17% of Informa's revenue in 2025, has spent recent years expanding beyond traditional academic publishing into open-access research, data and digital research services. ($1 = 0.7571 pounds)

item.title: Why Brazil could strip Enel of the power contract in its biggest city
item.description: Enel , one of the biggest utilities in Europe, on Tuesday faces a potential regulatory challenge to its lucrative contract to supply electricity to the largest city in the Southern Hemisphere.
item.dc:creator: Francesca Landini, Leticia Augusto
item.content:encoded: Enel (ENEI.MI) , one of the biggest utilities in Europe, on Tuesday faces a potential regulatory challenge to its lucrative contract to supply electricity to the largest city in the Southern Hemisphere. Brazil's electricity regulator, Aneel, has scheduled a meeting on October 6 to discuss whether to recommend termination of the Italian power company's licence to distribute electricity across metropolitan Sao Paulo before its 2028 expiry date. WHAT IS ANEEL DOING? The potential contract forfeiture is the harshest penalty Aneel can impose over a utility contract and has never been deployed before. The watchdog opened [USN:L1N448116 TEXT:"proceedings against Enel São Paulo"], Brazil's second-largest power distributor, in April. The business delivers electricity to about 8.5 million homes and businesses. Losing the concession would be one of the biggest regulatory shake-ups in the country's power sector in decades. WHAT LED TO THIS? Aneel cites a sustained pattern of failures after severe weather left millions of homes and businesses without power over the period from 2023 to 2025. In December 2025, power outages affected a cumulative total of 4.2 million homes and businesses, the watchdog said, representing more than half of Enel São Paulo's customer base. Enel says the proceedings focus on a single weather event in December 2025 and do not take into account improvements made over the past two and a half years, reaching fifth place in Brazil's service quality rankings in terms of average emergency response time, up from 31st place in 2023. Enel also disputes some of Aneel's methodology for calculating customer disruption and reconnection times. Enel has had to pay about 59 million reais ($11.8 million) in fines and undergone improvement plans, but 262 million reais remains unpaid due to court suspensions. WHAT NEXT? Aneel will discuss on Tuesday whether to recommend that Brazil's energy and mines ministry should revoke Enel's licence. The final decision rests with the ministry, but the government could instead take the case to Brazil's federal audit court to seek a mediated settlement with Enel. It is not clear how a runoff between right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in [USN:L6N45Q04L TEXT:"Brazil's presidential election"] this month could affect the final decision. WHY IS IT IMPORTANT? Brazil is Enel's largest market in Latin America. The group plans to invest about $5.3 billion in Brazil from 2026 to 2028, mostly in distribution networks, according to the Enel Americas business plan. Enel Sao Paulo generated about 3% of Enel Group's €22.9 billion total core profit in 2025. HOW MUCH IS THE CONTRACT WORTH? Assets relating to the contract were worth €3.9 billion ($4.4 billion) at the end of last year, including €595 million of goodwill. ($1 = 4.9934 reais) ($1 = 0.8921 euros)

item.title: US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dead at 86
item.description: U.S. televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, fraud conviction for bilking followers and divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Monday at age 86.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham
item.content:encoded: U.S. televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, fraud conviction for bilking followers and divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Monday at age 86. The death of Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media by his second wife, Lori Bakker. "It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening," she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband's latest television ministry. She paid tribute to Bakker as a "pioneer of Christian television," but the cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed. Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump, who was known for his own brand of right-wing populism. Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on U.S. television in the 1980s, achieving fame on the show "The PTL Club." PTL stood for "Praise The Lord" and "People That Love." Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should have stood for "pass the loot." Bakker spent 4-1/2 years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving vacations at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort. Prosecutors painted him as a selfish and petty con man driven by greed and lust for power. "Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests," Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing him. Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked. Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina. At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers on 200 TV stations and raked in $129 million a year. With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk. He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message - although it was larded with requests for money donations. Tammy Faye was more much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face. 'I HAVE SINNED' Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on all 24 fraud and conspiracy charges brought against him. Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158 million by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide. They said he siphoned $3.7 million to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants - and an air-conditioned dog house. The judge ordered Bakker to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. "I have sinned," Bakker told the court. "I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone." Bakker's chief aide, Richard Dortch, served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker. Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the trial - even singing to reporters after his conviction - but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007. Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the "prosperity gospel" he once preached and writing a book titled "I Was Wrong." "I've had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me," Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, who he married in 1998. They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping "The Jim Bakker Show" at a 600-acre (240-hectare) development called Morningside near the tourism city of Branson, Missouri, that bore similarities to Heritage USA. Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations. In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for COVID-19 during the deadly coronavirus pandemic. Bakker also said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first U.S. president to be impeached twice. James Orson Bakker was born on January 2, 1940, the son of an auto parts factory worker in Muskegon, Michigan, who maintained a strict fundamentalist Christian household. He met Tammy Faye LaValley at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis and they married in 1961. Both dropped out of school to become traveling evangelists as he pursued the career of a minister of the Pentecostalist Assemblies of God denomination. Their big break came in 1964, when televangelist Pat Robertson aired a children's religious puppet show with them on his fledgling TV network. Setting out on his own in the 1970s, Bakker used the emerging world of cable and satellite TV to build an empire.

item.title: Gauff hits out at racist abuse after replayed point in Beijing sparks backlash
item.description: Coco Gauff said she had received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after the two-times Grand Slam champion beat local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open on Monday in a match where a replayed point sparked an online backlash.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Coco Gauff said she had received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after the two-times Grand Slam champion beat local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open on Monday in a match where a replayed point sparked an online backlash. The American won 7-5 6-1 to reach the fourth round, but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set, raising her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner. After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed. Gauff won the replayed point and held serve for 5-5 before cruising to victory against the Chinese 16-year-old. Gauff, 22, said she had received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match. "You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff, who is Black, said on X early on Tuesday in reply to a post containing a racial slur. "The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane. "Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief." Reuters has contacted the WTA, the governing body of women's tennis, and tournament organisers in Beijing for comment. The WTA has made efforts to tackle the issue of online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system which monitors thousands of players and officials on social media. A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier. Gauff also explained that she was following the rules when she challenged the point. Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgment calls, including claims a distraction may have interfered with play. The American said she had spoken to Sun about the point at the end of the match. "Xinran's an incredible talent and player, I apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," she wrote. "I didn't like to see her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it's like but this is the beginning of an incredible career. It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd."

item.title: France's BPCE takes 7% stake in Sabadell, bolstering Spanish bank's defences
item.description: France's BPCE has bought a 7% stake in Spanish lender Sabadell and plans to be a long-term shareholder, in a move analysts said could help shield Sabadell from potential hostile bids after it fended off bigger rival BBVA last year.
item.dc:creator: Jesús Aguado
item.content:encoded: France's BPCE has bought a 7% stake in Spanish lender Sabadell (SABE.MC) and plans to be a long-term shareholder, in a move analysts said could help shield Sabadell from potential hostile bids after it fended off bigger rival BBVA (BBVA.MC) last year. The deal comes as [USN:L6N44O0MF TEXT:"European banking consolidation"] gathers pace, with Italy's [USN:L8N45L1OX TEXT:"UniCredit"] (CRDI.MI) moving closer to taking control of Germany's Commerzbank (CBKG.DE) . BPCE and Sabadell said on Tuesday they would explore opportunities for cooperation, particularly in corporate and investment banking and consumer credit. The two banks expect to conclude discussions in early 2027. They said any agreement would support Sabadell's growth in Spain while strengthening BPCE's presence in Europe. BPCE last year bought Portugal's Novo Banco for €6.4 billion ($7.4 billion). The banks did not disclose the value of the stake. At current market prices, a 7% holding in Sabadell is worth about €1.2 billion. At 0825 GMT, Sabadell shares were up 2.3%, outperforming Spain's blue-chip (.IBEX) index, which was up 1.2%. SABADELL'S STANDALONE STRATEGY Sabadell, Spain's fourth-largest bank by market value, is pursuing a standalone strategy following the [USN:L1N41E05M TEXT:"sale of British unit TSB"]. Analysts said the BPCE investment could form part of a defensive strategy after Sabadell entered last year's hostile takeover [USN:L5N3VX1KY TEXT:"battle with BBVA"] without significant core institutional shareholders, apart from insurer Zurich. "Obviously, this move removes possible situations such as the one experienced with BBVA. And the market will, in the long term, come to understand that the natural move would be a merger between the two, although this could take place only in the very long term," said Nuria Alvarez, an analyst at Madrid-based brokerage Renta 4. Sabadell said BPCE's stakebuilding had been agreed with the bank and carried out in a "friendly manner, with full transparency and clarity". It added that the deal does not envisage Sabadell taking a stake in the unlisted French lender. BPCE plans to seek representation on Sabadell's board and does not intend to increase its holding above 9.9%, according to a joint statement. Sabadell said the agreement does not envisage BPCE appointing a second board member. Citi analysts said "the arrival of a friendly strategic shareholder with board representation ambitions could nonetheless strengthen Sabadell's position in any future consolidation discussions." BPCE will begin talks with Spanish and European regulators on appointing a board representative, subject to the necessary approvals. ($1 = 0.8917 euros)

item.title: Spain's housing crisis bursts into the spotlight at snap election
item.description: Spain's snap election will revolve around an issue which has topped voters' list of concerns for three years straight but, until a fortnight ago, failed to dominate the political debate: housing.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Waldersee
item.content:encoded: Spain's [USN:L8N45R0GH TEXT:"snap election"] will revolve around an issue which has topped voters' list of concerns for three years straight but, until a fortnight ago, failed to dominate the political debate: housing. It was the [USN:L8N45F0PQ TEXT:"attempted eviction"] of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in central Madrid last month after her building was bought by a real estate firm that upended the country's politics. Her case triggered nationwide protests and catapulted the issue to the top of the agenda, even overshadowing immigration which had dominated headlines for weeks following a mass migrant crossing in Ceuta. Spain's housing shortage shares patterns with others across Europe: complex bureaucracy and labour shortages stalling supply, proliferating short-term rentals and high demand in urban centres pushing up prices, and rural areas hollowing out. From Ireland's 2024 election to Berlin's recent [USN:L8N4530I5 TEXT:"mayoral race"], the topic has particularly galvanised young voters across the region tired of spending a rising proportion of their incomes on rent. Yet how to resolve the crisis in Spain is a matter of bitter debate. 'TRUST US TO FIX IT' Housing plans proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialist government in Parliament last Friday [USN:S8N43C00Q TEXT:"were struck down"] by rightwing MPs who argued the measures - ranging from rent caps to limits on purchasing real estate for corporate entities - would worsen the problem by choking supply. Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the leader of the centre-right opposition People's Party, is pledging instead to build 250,000 new homes a year in projects creating 600,000 more jobs. "If Spaniards give me their trust, my priority, my success, will be housing policy," said Feijoo, whose party leads voting intention in September polls with around 33% support to the Socialist PSOE's 26%. Feijoo also wants to speed up urban planning to free up land for development and provide stronger mortgage and rental guarantees for young people. But some are sceptical about his promises. Marta, a 28-year-old Madrid resident and one of tens of thousands of protesters who took to the streets to voice discontent at the decree being struck down, hopes a successful election will strengthen the left's mandate to fix the issue. "If we leave this issue in the hands of the right, it's going to get much worse," she said. 'PASSING THE BUCK' Spain's regionalised structure often stands in the way. Central governments can set housing legislation and devise nationwide plans for incentives and subsidies, but their implementation, and wider urban planning, is largely devolved to regional governments and municipalities. All types of instruments - from rent controls proposed by the Socialists to eased planning permissions proposed by conservatives - have been struck down, blocked, or simply not implemented since the Socialists took power in 2018. Two decades on from a housing bubble and subsequent market collapse that scarred its economy, Spain's has flipped from a housing glut to a major deficit, estimated by its central bank at 750,000 homes and likely to reach a million by 2028. A steady recovery in demand, boosted by ultra-low interest rates and rising immigration, was not matched by new supply in the areas needing it most, as developers and lenders scarred by the crisis and lacking workers were loath to resume building. Though 73% of Spaniards own their homes, over half of 18-34 year olds now live with their parents or depend on them for living costs. House prices rose at three times the rate of wages last year, official statistics show, pushing more people to rent. At just 1.7% by European Commission calculations, its social housing stock is among the lowest in the EU. "Maricarmen was the tip of the iceberg. This situation has gone on forever, and all parties, the government and the regions, are to blame for passing the buck," said 40-year-old Alex Dominguez, a Madrid native living with his ex-girlfriend Marta because neither has found an affordable alternative since their breakup. 'VULTURE FUNDS' The Tenants' Union driving protests has called for a crackdown on "vulture funds", corporate investors it said were driving up prices and forcing evictions. The union has successfully intervened in several cases where properties were bought by institutional investors, negotiating compensation or preventing evictions like Maricarmen's. But Jorge Galindo, director of the Centre for Economic Policy EsadeEcPol, argued that aggressive government action against private investors would chill construction projects. "The (government) decrees create a tradeoff between protecting those already in rent and facilitating supply for those who haven't yet found a place to live," Galindo said. Land registry data also shows institutional ownership outside densely populated cities like Madrid is minimal. Just 4.4% of homes nationwide are owned by companies and 4.3% of landlords have 11 or more properties on the market, an amount that subjects them to stricter regulations. Some 40% of homes for rent belong to individual landlords with just one property on the market who supplement wages with rental income, according to the Bank of Spain. Political analyst Cristina Monge said that meant successful government policies had to balance the interests of homeowners who make up three-quarters of the populace and renters, a smaller but growing and more vulnerable group. "Property owners see their own children struggling to access housing - not just to buy, but even to rent," she said. "That is what makes housing policy so complex now; if we were a country with a higher percentage of renters, the policies required might be simpler to devise." Still, for some of the protesters who marched in Madrid, radical steps are needed. "We need a bit of humanity in how we deal with this," said Marta, Alex's ex-girlfriend. "Housing is a right."

item.title: Trump orders firing squad for gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas
item.description: The gunman described the shooting spree as retaliation for US wars in the Muslim world.
item.dc:creator: Phil Stewart, Steve Gorman
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad to execute the former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree the gunman later described as retaliation for US wars in the Muslim world, the Pentagon said on Monday. Putting former US Army Major Nidal Hasan to death by Army firing squad was approved by Trump at the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X. Parnell noted that Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar" — God is greatest in Arabic — during the attack, which killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others. The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution, Parnell said, adding, "Judgment day for Hasan has finally come." Death by firing squad was one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times. Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel [USN:L1N45O0WH TEXT:"botched"] an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but unconscious and hospitalized on life support. Pike's lawyers had previously urged that the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection, such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners faced in establishing a sound intravenous line. A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base. The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police upon his arrest. In a statement responding to Trump's decision, the group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said: "There is nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill." Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of Military Justice a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out "until approved by the president." If Hasan is put to death, it would mark the first military execution since 1961, the group said. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad was one carried out "by musketry" in November 1945, the center reported. At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

item.title: India detains opposition lawmakers protesting against election chief
item.description: Indian police detained several opposition lawmakers in the capital of New Delhi on Tuesday for trying to breach barricades during a protest march to demand the resignation of the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma
item.content:encoded: Indian police detained several opposition lawmakers in the capital of New Delhi on Tuesday for trying to breach barricades during a protest march to demand the resignation of the election chief over a [USN:L4N45K0E7 TEXT:"controversial revision"] of voter lists. The march presents a fresh political challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar protests forced the resignation of his [USN:L1N43R02E TEXT:"education minister"] over exam paper leaks. Parties opposing Modi's government along with members of the popular 'cockroach' youth movement protested against Chief Election Commissioner [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] after the Indian Express newspaper reported divisions in the poll body last month. The reported differences over the lists and voter registration procedures stoked concern about the neutrality of the commission, led by a Modi government appointee. "The election commission is a puppet in the hands of the government," Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge, told reporters as the march began. "We are fighting to save our democracy." MARCHERS CARRY PLACARDS, FLAGS, SHOUT SLOGANS Lawmakers carried placards, waved the national flag, and shouted slogans against Kumar during the march, roughly 1-km-long, or less than a mile, to the Election Commission headquarters from parliament, through the centre of Delhi. Some carried placards calling Kumar a traitor and accused the BJP of snatching away the right to vote, while they sat on the road outside the panel's office, demanding to meet him. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka and several more stood on police barricades there, waving the national flag and calling for Kumar to resign. Hundreds of security personnel, some wearing riot gear and carrying batons, tried to stop Gandhi and other lawmakers from entering the election commission. Police did not immediately comment on the detentions. PROTESTS PUSH ANARCHY, BJP SAYS "After failing multiple times, Congress leaders have decided to establish anarchy in the country and attack institutions," BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra told reporters before Tuesday's protest. TV channels said the Gandhi siblings were among those briefly detained before being released. The duo sought entry through the grounds of the state radio office next door, where they sat in protest under a tree after the route was blocked, the channels said. Congress and other parties say the revised voter lists benefit Modi and his party. Kumar has not commented on the issue, but the commission and Modi's BJP denied the accusations. Tuesday's event is the [USN:L1N45O03D TEXT:"latest"] of a series of almost daily demonstrations by student organisations, political parties and the 'cockroach' movement, which began last week. India's Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear requests for its intervention in the accusations against the poll body's voter drive, and the conduct of its chief. If "there are decisions against the law ... We will take care of it," the court said at the hearing, after the petitioners accused the poll body of bias.

item.title: India tractor sales weaken as poor monsoon hurts farm demand
item.description: India's September tractor retail sales declined 12.6% from a month earlier as the worst monsoon in a decade and a delayed festive season weighed on farm equipment demand, even as broader auto sales stayed resilient, a dealers' body said on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Kashish Tandon, Saikeerthi .
item.content:encoded: India's September tractor retail sales declined 12.6% from a month earlier as the worst monsoon in a decade and a delayed festive season weighed on farm equipment demand, even as broader auto sales stayed resilient, a dealers' body said on Tuesday. Tractor sales fell to 76,906 units in September from 87,977 in August, according to data from the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations. The decline comes as the June-September monsoon, which delivers nearly 70% of India's annual rainfall, was [USN:P8N43X0AN TEXT:"12.6% below"] normal this year, fuelling concerns over crop yields, rural demand and food inflation in Asia's third-largest economy. Historically, September and October have been the strongest months for tractor wholesales, but a later-than-usual festive season and below-normal rainfall have hurt demand this year, said Yash Agrawal, an auto analyst at brokerage Nirmal Bang. "Over-reliance on weather conditions is higher for tractors because they are directly impacted by crop production and overall cash flow of farmers," Agrawal said. The slowdown could have wider implications for automakers including Mahindra & Mahindra (MAHM.NS) and Escorts Kubota (ESCO.NS) , as tractors are among their highest-margin businesses. FADA President Sai Giridhar said the weakness was largely confined to tractors, arguing that rural vehicle demand was increasingly detached from farm incomes as non-agricultural businesses and employment gain prominence. "Only the tractor segment is directly linked to farm income," Giridhar said, adding that rural sales of passenger and commercial vehicles as well as two-wheelers were growing at a pace comparable with, or exceeding, urban sales. Overall retail sales of two-wheelers, passenger and commercial vehicles rose 31.8% year-on-year and nearly 5% from the previous month to 2.54 million units. Dealers' sentiment was upbeat heading into the festive season, with more than three-fourths in a survey expecting sales to grow in October, supported by healthy enquiries, the dealers' body said.

item.title: Gulf oil flows rise to average 81% of pre-war rate in September, data shows
item.description: Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre-war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports despite attacks on the kingdom's oil infrastructure and escalating Iranian attacks on regional shipping, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade.
item.dc:creator: Ahmad Ghaddar
item.content:encoded: Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre-war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports despite attacks on the kingdom's oil infrastructure and escalating Iranian attacks on regional shipping, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade. The blockade has all but choked off Iranian exports, while other Gulf producers have adapted to attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping by relying on so-called dark transits — switching off tankers' tracking systems to evade detection — to protect the oil flows that underpin their economies. Flows of crude, condensate and refined fuels including LPG averaged 19.2 million barrels per day (bpd) from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Iraq and the UAE, Vortexa data showed, compared with an average of about 23.6 million bpd in the year that preceded the outbreak of the Iran war on February 28. Data from Kpler showed total September oil exports at 18.6 million bpd. CRUDE EXPORTS POST LARGER RECOVERY, PRODUCTS LAG Crude and condensate flows recovered to 91% of their pre-war levels of 16.3 million bpd, Vortexa data showed. But exports of refined fuels, including LPG, remain at 60% of their pre-war levels of 7.3 million bpd. The decline in fuel exports has exacerbated global shortages of diesel and jet fuel, contributing to record or near-record prices in several markets. The Middle East is a key supplier of such fuels, making regional disruptions particularly significant for global consumers. "Daily flows are considerably more volatile than before the war, so the key question is whether recent levels can be sustained," Vortexa analyst Claire Jungman said. According to Kpler data, Saudi Arabia drove a sharp recovery in overall Gulf crude and condensate exports in September, with shipments rising by about 4.2 million bpd from August to 6.6 million bpd. Drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West Pipeline last month, [USN:L1N45E09V TEXT:"temporarily halting"] crude loadings at the kingdom's Yanbu oil port on the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia's rebound more than offset declines elsewhere in the Gulf, accounting for all of the region's net export growth and more, as exports recovered from disruptions that had depressed flows in previous months. Kpler data showed combined crude and condensate exports from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar and Iran rose to about 14.7 million bpd in September from 10.8 million bpd in August. The rebound came even as Iranian exports fell to zero and exports from Kuwait and Qatar declined. Higher Saudi shipments more than offset those losses, while exports from the UAE and Iraq also increased.

item.title: Euro trades around 17-month low amid French debt worries, dollar steady
item.description: The euro steadied just above a 17-month low on Tuesday as euro zone bond markets stabilised, a day after the currency fell sharply on fears that stress in French bond markets could spread more widely.
item.dc:creator: Rae Wee, Harry Robertson
item.content:encoded: The euro steadied just above a 17-month low on Tuesday as euro zone bond markets stabilised, a day after the currency fell sharply on fears that stress in French bond markets could spread more widely. The US dollar continued to trade at around its highest since April 2025, meanwhile, supported by rising US Treasury yields. The euro was down less than 0.1% at $1.12, having slid to its lowest since May 2025 in the previous session at $1.116, extending its more than 1% drop from last week. The common currency has come under pressure due to worries about [USN:L6N45O0HP TEXT:"high debt levels"] and political gridlock in France, with an upcoming [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"snap election in Spain"] adding to headwinds. A sliding euro is also the [USN:L8N45R0QJ TEXT:"latest warning sign"] for policymakers as surging French borrowing costs ripple across the broader euro zone. "We're pretty pessimistic about the euro. We think it's going to go down to under $1.10," said Joseph Capurso, a strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. "For the euro to rise, you'd need a big decrease in oil prices," he said. "Another one would be them (France) starting to get their act together on reining in the budget deficit, though I think there's no chance of that happening anytime soon." French bond yields fell almost 0.1 percentage points on Tuesday as oil prices dipped slightly, easing some of the worries about a spiralling debt selloff. Yields move inversely to prices. In the broader market, the dollar stayed strong, drawing support from still-elevated US Treasury yields, which scaled multi-decade highs on Monday. The dollar index was last little changed at 102.16, having scaled an 18-month high of 102.53 in the previous session. The greenback's strength has come despite reduced expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike this month in the wake of [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"weaker-than-expected"] US jobs data, as investors bet the central bank would still need to tighten policy further. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, the chance of a hike in October is at 22%, while it rises to around 85% for December. "The dollar has continued to find support at the start of this week," said Francesco Pesole, currency strategist at ING. "The euro’s idiosyncratic weakness is still playing a role, and so are global bond yields that keep pushing higher." Data on Monday showed the US services-sector activity [USN:S0N44H007 TEXT:"slowed in September"], with strong domestic demand stretching supply chains and raising prices paid by businesses for inputs, indicating that inflation could remain high into next year. Against the yen, the dollar rose 0.2% to 158.21 , while sterling was little changed at $1.323. The Bank of Japan may [USN:L4N45S011 TEXT:"signal this month"] that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2% target, three sources familiar with its thinking said, highlighting its readiness to raise interest rates again in the coming months. Elsewhere, the Australian dollar slipped 0.1% to $0.696.

item.title: Cornell students stage anti-rape rally in support of 'Jane Doe'
item.description: Cornell University students staged a mass rally voicing solidarity with a classmate whose gang-rape allegations have ignited a national uproar and demanding that the Ivy League school take firmer action against sexual violence on campus.
item.dc:creator: Ed Ou, Steve Gorman
item.content:encoded: Cornell University students staged a mass rally on Monday voicing solidarity with a classmate whose [USN:L1N45O0OO TEXT:"gang-rape allegations"] have ignited a national uproar and demanding that the Ivy League school take firmer action against sexual violence on campus. The protesters called for an external inquiry into how Cornell's administration has handled the matter, independent hearings and uniform minimum sanctions for all sexual assaults on campus, and better training for campus police in responding to complaints of sexual violence and harassment. The alleged gang-rape victim, identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe, has said the university failed to adequately investigate and punish campus fraternity members who were involved. Some demonstrators also called for the resignation of Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other members of his administration, saying their policies have perpetuated what protesters called a "culture of rape" on campus. In a lawsuit filed last month, Jane Doe said she was plied with drugs and alcohol and then sexually assaulted by several members of the campus chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024 after she had become incapacitated. Doe, who was 20 at the time, named seven Chi Phi members as defendants in the suit, along with the fraternity chapter, a local bar, her own sorority, and the university. She had reported the alleged assault to police several weeks after the fact, leading to an internal university investigation and a law enforcement probe, but the local prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges in the case. Cornell, which has defended its response to the original report, shut down the Chi Phi chapter and imposed a range of discipline on the fraternity members involved, including expulsions and other sanctions. The men all denied any wrongdoing, some saying the sexual activity was consensual and others disputing their participation, the New York Times has reported, citing Cornell documents. The lawsuit criticized the university for having offered some of the alleged perpetrators a chance to mitigate their penalties by writing essays. The demonstrators on Monday demanded that Cornell expel or revoke the degrees of any student found complicit in the alleged gang rape. 'PRISON SENTENCES, NOT TOPIC SENTENCES' New York Governor Kathy Hochul last Friday appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor to take over a newly reopened criminal investigation, saying she was "deeply disturbed" by how local authorities originally dealt with the case. Monday's boisterous but orderly demonstration included a march by several hundred students, faculty supporters and community activists — perhaps 1,000 or more — through the campus in the upstate New York town of Ithaca. The protesters, chanting "One struggle, one fight" and "No justice, no peace," filled the central pedestrian plaza on campus, and spilled over into adjacent spaces. Many carried signs with slogans such as "Justice for Jane Doe," "We Stand for Survivors" and "Prison Sentences, not Topic Sentences." The march ended at Cornell's main administration building, which was defaced in Monday's predawn hours by unknown activists who smashed two glass panes of the front door and spray-painted graffiti on the entryway, including one message that read: "AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED." Independent student newspaper the Cornell Daily Sun reported receiving a statement from the activists saying their vandalism was an act of protest of the alleged assault and "global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place." The rally came a day after Doe and her lawyer said they had [USN:L6N45Q09V TEXT:"received multiple threats"] since filing the lawsuit, which has prompted a public outcry, particularly on social media under the banner "#IamJaneDoe," over why law enforcement declined to pursue charges in 2024. The uproar also stirred a backlash by others who have questioned whether keeping Doe anonymous was fair because it denied those implicated in the matter the chance to publicly face their accuser. Addressing the controversy on Saturday, Kotlikoff promised in a video message to examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus, saying, "being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility."

item.title: Australian soldier killed, five injured when vehicle rolls over in training
item.description: An Australian soldier has died and five others have been injured when a vehicle rolled over during a training exercise, the country's army said on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An Australian soldier has died and five others have been injured when a vehicle rolled over during a training exercise, the country's army said on Tuesday. The Australian Army identified the soldier as Corporal Brendan Hannam, a father of two and an Afghanistan veteran. Hannam was a passenger in a vehicle that rolled over on October 5 at the Mount Bundey Training Area near Darwin, the Northern Territory's capital, it said. Of the five who were injured, two were in a stable condition in hospital in Darwin and three were being monitored at the army barracks. Lieutenant General Susan Coyle, chief of Australia's army, said Hannam was a "much beloved" soldier who had served on two operational tours to Afghanistan in 2019 and trained Ukrainians with the British Armed Forces in the UK. "His mates tell me that he would give the shirt off his back for anybody," Coyle told a news conference. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a post on social media the incident was a "terrible reminder of what families take on when their loved one bravely puts on our nation's uniform". It was the second death during training in recent months. An Australian Special Air Service Regiment soldier was killed during a parachute training exercise in May.

item.title: US envoy attends event with Sudanese army chief in Egypt
item.description: An envoy of President Donald Trumpsaid he attended an event over the weekend with the head of Sudan's army, which is fighting a war with paramilitary forces that has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: An envoy of President Donald Trump said he attended an event over the weekend with the head of Sudan's army, which is fighting a war with paramilitary forces that has created one of the world's [USN:L6N45M0KU TEXT:"worst humanitarian crises"]. DETAILS: US Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos said on X he attended a lunch hosted by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi alongside Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. "We ... reaffirm the United States' continued efforts, alongside our Egyptian partners and our other regional and international partners and allies, to advance a political solution to the crisis," Boulos added in his post. A senior official in Sudan's military-led government said Burhan had a "casual encounter" with Boulos, but the two did not hold any talks. The event in Egypt came less than two weeks after Washington [USN:L6N45E0RI TEXT:"withheld a visa"] for the Sudanese army chief ahead of a scheduled UN appearance, in a move that Sudanese and other sources said was linked to a US-backed ceasefire proposal that Khartoum has resisted. Sudan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when the two fell out over issues including how to integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule. The US State Department said last month that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary nor either of their respective leaders "represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan". The war has displaced more than 14 million people and unleashed waves of ethnically driven killings . "The United States stands ready to support all efforts leading to a comprehensive dialogue among the Sudanese political forces, leading to a preliminary road map of the future of the Sudan," Boulos said on Monday. Washington [USN:L6N45M0KU TEXT:"has accused"] the RSF of committing genocide and the army of carrying out war crimes. Both have previously denied abuses.

item.title: Jeffrey Archer, UK novelist and scandal-plagued politician, dies on eve of final book
item.description: Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, died aged 86 on Monday, just one day before his final novel "Adam and Eve" was due to be published.
item.dc:creator: Sam Tobin
item.content:encoded: Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, died aged 86 on Monday, just one day before his final novel "Adam and Eve" was due to be published. The confidant of former prime minister Margaret Thatcher lived a life that swung from the heights of luxury and fame to the lows of a two-year stint in prison for perjury over paying a woman for sex. He sold more than 300 million copies of his books, spent a total of five and a half years on the New York Times bestseller lists and found fans around the world with his pacy thrillers, among them the 1976 debut "Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less" and 1979's mass-selling "Kane & Abel". Publisher HarperCollins said Archer, who had met and signed books for fans in London's Leicester Square Theatre on Sunday and had been scheduled to speak at events this week, died "suddenly and peacefully at home ... between writing sessions". "We're all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend," said Kate Elton, HarperCollins' UK CEO and Archer's editor. "When he set out to write 'Adam and Eve', he told me from the very beginning that it would be his final novel". HEAVY DEBTS CURTAILED HIS LIFE AS A LAWMAKER Archer first made headlines when he entered parliament in 1969, aged 29, before he became a casualty of a fraudulent investment scheme which meant he did not stand for re-election in 1974 but went into writing to try to clear his debts. "When I was three, I wanted to be four; when I was four, I wanted to be prime minister," he was quoted as saying in 2001. Despite only a short stint in parliament, he remained a central figure within the Conservative Party, spent more than 30 years sitting in the upper House of Lords chamber in parliament and raised millions of pounds for charity. Cabinet ministers and celebrities flocked to his "champagne and shepherd's pie" parties, with guests recalling how anyone looking for the bathroom at his London apartment was told to "Go past the Picasso and turn left at the Matisse". Some of that interest waned with his very public downfall. In 1987, Archer sued the Daily Star tabloid for saying he had paid a woman for sex, winning a then-record £500,000 ($660,450) in damages. The case returned to the public eye when he was selected as the Conservative candidate to become London's first elected mayor in 1999. A former friend accused him of lying and Archer was eventually charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice, convicted and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He served two years, during which time he wrote "A Prison Diary". ARCHER TRIAL NOTORIOUS FOR JUDGE'S SUMMING UP The trial became notorious for the judge's summing up of evidence given by Archer's wife Mary. "Remember Mary Archer in the witness box," the judge, Bernard Caulfield, told the jury. "Your vision of her will probably never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance?" And, of Archer, he added: "Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel?" The fall from grace did no harm to his literary career. HarperCollins said Archer's books were sold in 119 countries and he was due to speak at an event in London on Wednesday and the Cheltenham Literature Festival this weekend. Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the Conservatives, said she was shocked by the news, having received a message from Archer as she attended her annual party conference on Monday morning saying: "great outfit, great speech, no need to reply". Asked recently by the BBC why he wanted "Adam and Eve" to be his last book, Archer said: "It's been 50 very happy years. But there is always a time. I think the clever thing in life is when to get out." ($1 = 0.7571 pounds)

item.title: French bond contagion fears are rattling the euro
item.description: A sliding euro is the latest alarm bell for policymakers facing a surge in French borrowing costs that has started to spill over into the broader euro area.
item.dc:creator: Dhara Ranasinghe, Alun John
item.content:encoded: A sliding euro is the latest alarm bell for policymakers facing a surge in French borrowing costs that has started to spill over into the broader euro area. The euro hit [USN:L1N45R03D TEXT:"17-month lows below $1.12"] on Monday and tumbled against sterling , the Swiss franc and Japan's yen . France is at the heart of the European market concerns. The French government is seeking to enact an unpopular [USN:L1N45N0A3 TEXT:"2027 budget"] to lower its deficit and contain its record-high debt load, a tall order in a deeply divided parliament as political factions position ahead of next year's presidential election. Investors, unwilling to take chances, are [USN:L8N45O0S7 TEXT:"dumping French bonds"] while buying safe German debt. With the premium investors demand to hold French over German government bonds now at its [USN:L8N45O0YO TEXT:"highest since"] the 2010-2012 euro zone debt crisis, currency markets fear contagion. At stake is feeble economic expansion in a bloc rocked by political uncertainty. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party last month suffered the worst regional election defeat in postwar Germany. And on Monday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"snap election"]. Italy also holds elections next year. With inflation already rising on soaring energy costs and higher yields increasing household and corporate borrowing costs, further euro weakening could leave the European Central Bank caught between fighting inflation and calming bond markets. The French/German 10-year bond yield gap last week saw its biggest weekly jump in decades, while the gap between Italian and German yields hit almost 130 basis points (bps), posting its biggest weekly rise since the COVID-19 crisis. "The bond sell-off is seeing bigger moves in anything that is perceived in any way, shape, or form as more vulnerable, and that has seen an outbreak of euro selling that's gathered momentum," said Societe Generale's chief FX strategist Kit Juckes. "The factors that held euro/dollar above key levels through the summer... I think that's gone," he said, pointing to earlier assumptions of a short-lived energy shock and a US push to weaken the dollar. NEW DIMENSION TO EURO WEAKNESS While the euro is comfortably above 20-year lows hit in 2022 when Russia's invasion of Ukraine sparked an energy crisis, the bond market moves add a new dimension to euro weakness. Every further 10 bps widening in the French spread against Germany would be associated with a 0.4% fall in euro/dollar, BofA FX strategists estimate. "The typical response is closer to zero most of the time, but (the spread impact) can rise significantly in times of acute stress," Goldman Sachs analysts said in a note. "Spreads do not matter for the currency until they are the only thing that matters," they said, adding that the impact on the euro rises when a risk event pushes German yields down, but those elsewhere in the bloc higher. This was the case last week when Germany's Bund yield fell almost 17 bps, its biggest weekly drop since 2024 . "Euro/dollar is usually influenced more from the dollar side, but this time there is an impact from Europe too," said Amundi Asset Management's head of global FX Andreas König. "You have to go back a bit in time to when European headlines last made the euro move," he said. König did not see a turnaround in the medium term and was sticking with a dollar overweight position given the US growth and rate outlook. CFTC positioning data show traders positioned for a fall in the euro, a view also reflected in currency options. Three-month euro risk reversals , which reflect the difference between the cost of an option to buy the euro against the cost of one to sell it, fell on Friday to their most bearish since 2024. Analysts said the euro could test $1.10, while SocGen's Juckes also highlighted euro vulnerability against the likes of the yen and Swiss franc. The euro fell almost 4% against the yen in September. A falling currency alongside bond market stress means talk has turned to how policymakers could stabilise markets, especially if 2027's French election causes more strain. The ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument allows it to buy an unlimited number of bonds from a country experiencing an "unwarranted, disorderly" tightening of financing conditions. For now, growth, though weak, has strengthened. Euro zone business activity expanded at its fastest pace in nearly 3-1/2 years in September, S&P Global data showed. The degree to which banks, the main financiers of companies in the region, can keep lending to their economies is also in focus. "If the fiscal contagion risk in Europe is not contained, I can see euro/dollar trading lower, despite the fact that it was already slightly undervalued," said Stephen Jen, CEO and co-CIO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management.

item.title: Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi after injuring spectator with ball
item.description: Russian Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final clash with Novak Djokovic after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd, striking a spectator in the eye.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russian Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final clash with Novak Djokovic after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd, striking a spectator in the eye. World number five Medvedev was trailing 7-5 5-3 on Monday and had lost a point when he hit the ball coming off the wall. The spectator, who was sitting in the first row behind Medvedev, clutched his left eye and appeared to be in pain as he walked out of the gallery, assisted by stadium staff. Medvedev did not protest the umpire's decision to disqualify him. The Russian will lose his points and prize money from the tournament as a result of the default. "Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all," Medvedev told reporters." I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels." The 30-year-old former US Open champion said he did not cause the incident intentionally. "The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn't go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don't think I was ever close to such a situation." Sixth seed Djokovic said he was shocked by the incident. "I hope that person is not badly injured," said Djokovic, who was disqualified from the US Open in 2020 in similar circumstances. "On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match." Both semi-finals ended prematurely in Beijing as Hubert Hurkacz retired with an adductor injury earlier in the day. Australian Alex de Minaur was leading the first semi 6-4 3-2 when his Polish opponent, who had struggled with movement throughout the match, retired. 'GRUELLING BATTLE' Djokovic's win extended his China Open record to 33 victories without a loss, extending his record of making the best start in a men's singles tournament in the Open Era. The Serbian beat French and U.S. Open champion Alexander Zverev [USN:L6N45Q056 TEXT:"in the quarter-finals"] to break the record Rafael Nadal set by winning his first 31 matches at Roland Garros. Djokovic, 39, survived punishing long rallies and saved seven break points to take the first set in one hour and 19 minutes. He was serving for the match when Medvedev was disqualified. "It was a gruelling battle ... it always is a big battle with Daniil and it's so hard to play him," said Djokovic, who won the tournament all six times he played in it from 2009 to 2015 before returning to the event this year. "Another final. There's something about Beijing that just keeps me going."

item.title: BT’s vulture M&A dials up a worthwhile connection
item.description: The £20 bln UK telecom group said it had bought loss-making TalkTalk out of administration. Boosting its already big market share raises antitrust risks, yet the UK government’s blessing may help. A lowball price, plus likely synergies, means shareholders may not be left hanging.
item.dc:creator: Neil Unmack
item.content:encoded: Allison Kirkby is looking like Britain’s answer to Jamie Dimon. The BT (BT.L) CEO has just stepped in to buy up the carcass of indebted telecom group TalkTalk, just as JPMorgan (JPM.N) boss is known for saving weak US banks. It looks like a risky move: TalkTalk is lossmaking, and the deal could raise antitrust risks, although Kirkby’s shareholders can probably emerge happy. TalkTalk may create a new motto in European leveraged finance: never lend to UK telco buyouts. The group was already in turnaround mode when Toscafund took it private in 2020: it relied heavily on the BT-owned network Openreach to sell broadband, giving it little pricing power in an increasingly competitive market. In recent years, high debt and dwindling customers has seen its profitability collapse. It had been kept afloat by chief lender Ares Management (ARES.N) , which has over the years put over £500 million in debt and equity into the group. TalkTalk’s dire financial status made rescuing it increasingly challenging. Any buyer would have needed to fund operating losses, invest in new customer service, and pay arrears and future network charges to Openreach. That makes BT a logical acquirer, as more than half of TalkTalk’s revenue goes straight to Openreach, which would be lost if the group went bust. The outlay for BT is around £400 million, including the non-receipt of some £100 million of Openreach charges. The remainder will go to Ares, which will recover some £100 million in high-ranking senior lending and more in fees, and asset-backed lender KKR (KKR.N) . It will also cover costs. But the rest of TalkTalk’s debt, which Fitch Ratings estimates at £1.5 billion in total, will face steep losses. TalkTalk's 8.25% bond, issued in 2025, was trading at just 2 pence in the pound on Monday. Buying TalkTalk out of administration makes sense, but it’s still risky for Kirkby. BT’s share of the UK retail market may now exceed 35%, raising the risk that the UK Competition and Markets Authority unwinds the deal or forces disposals. Prime Minister Andy Burnham appears to have panicked at the prospect of 1 million customers losing broadband access overnight if TalkTalk went into liquidation, and granted a public interest intervention notice, which should tame the CMA. Still, rival operators will petition for remedies: Virgin Media 02 has called the deal a “ stitch-up ”. The deal maths looks sound for BT, providing some cushion. It can make savings by slashing costs and selling more products. Assume synergies of perhaps half Talk Talk’s operating costs, equivalent to £150 million pounds, and the savings' present value alone, after tax and capitalised on a multiple of 10, would exceed £1 billion, more than double the initial outlay. And saving TalkTalk avoids the risk of BT's broadband customers vanishing or going to a rival. The TalkTalk saga may prompt changes. A clearer administration regime should allow ailing broadband providers to avoid the risk of customers being switched off. And broadband companies may need to operate with lower debt. BT may benefit from the deal, but in an ideal world the telecom group should never have needed to step in in the first place. Follow @Unmack1 on X. BT Group on October 5 announced it had bought the main businesses of the TalkTalk group out of administration. The transaction, which will see BT take on TalkTalk’s 1.5 million retail customers, will result in a “cash impact” of £400 million, BT said in a statement. That figure includes the “non-receipt” of £100 million owed to BT by TalkTalk. BT shares rose by 1.7% to 199 pence as of 1046 GMT on October 5. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Oil's new problem isn't supply. It's logistics
item.description: Middle East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: Middle East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the [USN:S8N43Z003 TEXT:"Strait of Hormuz"] – despite the continued threat of Iranian attacks. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses. Crude flows through the embattled waterway reached 14.2 million barrels per day on a seven-day average on Sept. 26, nearly 80% of pre-war levels, according to analytics firm Kpler. While volumes have declined since, they will likely be revised higher because ships often disable satellite tracking systems while traversing the strait and for several days thereafter. Either way, the trend is clear: a lot more crude is getting through the strait. So why is Brent still trading above $100 per barrel? In a word, logistics. For decades, the global oil industry functioned as a finely tuned system designed to move enormous volumes of crude and fuels over long distances at the lowest possible cost. The conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe have fractured that model, as a combination of record-high tanker rates, soaring insurance costs and a severe shortage of refining capacity has created bottlenecks across the energy supply chain. Those problems may take months, if not years, to unwind, leaving consumers facing persistently high energy bills – even if the crude supply squeeze continues to ease. BREAKING THE BLOCKADE Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following the onset of the war with the US and Israel on February 28 rapidly reshaped global oil flows. Gulf producers diverted supplies through alternative routes, buyers sought barrels from more distant regions and governments released unprecedented volumes of oil from strategic reserves. One of the biggest changes was that Saudi Arabia – previously the world’s largest oil exporter – diverted its exports through its [USN:L4N45E0KG TEXT:"East-West pipeline"], which delivers crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. At one point this year, 4% of global oil supplies were via this route. However, after the pipeline came under attack by Iranian-backed Iraqi militias [USN:L6N4590XN TEXT:"in early September"], Saudi Arabia was forced to redirect exports back to the Gulf via Hormuz, which it discovered, could be more easily transited than previously thought. Saudi exports through Hormuz averaged 3 million bpd in September, the highest level during the conflict, according to Kpler. While Saudi Arabia’s crude exports through Hormuz in September were still only around half of pre-war volumes, the Kingdom’s exports could quickly near pre-war levels as the East-West pipeline [USN:L4N45E0KG TEXT:"gradually returns"] to normal operations.
